newsitem.title: BELARUS: Way ahead unclear for Russia-Belarus union hopes.
newsitem.headline: Way ahead unclear for Russia-Belarus union hopes.

text.p: The peoples of Russia and Belarus ran out of time on Thursday in six weeks of public debate requested by their presidents on how to re-establish ties broken when the Soviet Union fell apart.
No clear view emerged what shape a new union might take.

Even the two presidents -- Russia's Boris Yeltsin and Belarus's Alexander Lukashenko -- have not agreed how to move ahead as promised in nine days time from the skeleton treaty and draft charter they put forward on April 2.

Belarus, its population of 10 million dwarfed by Russia's 150 million, has no weighty modern history as an independent nation and the great majority of its people speak Russian, not the closely related local language, in daily life.

Although the idea of restoring bonds between Minsk and Moscow has broad support in both countries, the "public debate" on how was mostly an official affair conducted by experts, politicians and a few activists in television studios and the newspapers.
But vociferous Belarus nationalists -- who seem to be a small minority -- have staged a series of protests opposing Lukashenko's plans for union and accusing Russian leaders of imperial schemes.
Officials in both countries reported opinion surveys indicating substantial majorities in favour of the general idea of union.
But when Yeltsin said in an interview on Wednesday that he favoured a merger, the word set alarm bells ringing in Minsk, where Lukashenko seeks a link that will retain two equal, sovereign states.

Belarus's economic and political life have changed much less than Russia's since the collapse of communism and Lukashenko's authoritarian rule and bad human rights record have made him a pariah to the West.
Pro-Western liberals in the Kremlin are wary of any deal which would set the Belarus leader on a par with Yeltsin and give him significant influence over Russia.
Critics say he is mainly interested in a larger stage to act on -- with his eye on Russia's next presidential election in three years' time.
Russian negotiators say the Belarus side had shown reluctance to allow too close a union while Moscow was insisting that the document included the ultimate goal of creating a single federation.
Mikhail Podgainy, a senior member of Lukashenko's administration, said no single aspect of the charter had won unanimous support in five opinion polls in Belarus.

"Proposals are often mutually exclusive, and a significant number of people who took part in the debate had not read the charter," he said, adding that 59.4 percent wanted a union, 15.7 percent opposed it and 12.2 percent were categorically against.

Russia's Deputy Prime Minister Valery Serov told Itar-Tass news agency the draft had won popular approval, with 72 percent of Russians for integration and 10 percent against. Yeltsin said on television that 80 percent were in favour. Neither said where their figures came from.
